title: Wiggle Sort II
summary: Reorder nums in place so adjacent comparisons alternate strictly less-than and greater-than, beginning with nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2].
statement: Reorder nums in place so adjacent comparisons alternate strictly less-than and greater-than, beginning with nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2]. Keep every value occurrence and return nothing. A valid arrangement is guaranteed to exist.
constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 50000; 0 <= nums[i] <= 5000. A strict wiggle arrangement is guaranteed to exist.

Modify the original list so nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3] and so on. Keep every input occurrence exactly once; adjacent equality is NOT allowed. Return nothing. Any valid arrangement is accepted.
The baseline target allows sorting with O(n) workspace. Linear-time and constant-extra-space partitioning are optional follow-ups.
reference_solution:
def wiggle_sort_strict(nums):
    ordered = sorted(nums)
    middle = (len(nums)+1)//2
    nums[::2] = ordered[:middle][::-1]
    nums[1::2] = ordered[middle:][::-1]
hints: Repeated values must be separated; the simple one-pass non-strict Wiggle Sort algorithm is insufficient.
After sorting, place the smaller half at even valley positions and the larger half at odd peak positions, traversing BOTH halves backward.
Let middle=(n+1)//2. Assign sorted[:middle] reversed to nums[::2], and sorted[middle:] reversed to nums[1::2].
Backward placement separates repeated median values. Under the guaranteed-feasible input contract every adjacent peak is strictly larger than its valleys.
editorial: Split sorted values into a lower half (including the median for odd lengths) and an upper half. Fill even and odd positions from the ends of these halves. Upper values dominate lower values; reversing prevents equal median occurrences from becoming adjacent in feasible instances. The property judge checks both the complete multiset and strict alternation, so multiple arrangements pass. The independent oracle uses multiset backtracking to find a legal permutation on small inputs. This contract differs from Wiggle Sort, where equality is allowed.

tests.explanation: One valid arrangement is [1,4,1,5,1,6]: each 1 is below its neighboring peaks. [1,6,1,5,1,4] is equally valid.
One valid arrangement is [2,3,1,3,1,2]. Simply interleaving sorted halves forward can place two 2s next to each other, which fails the strict rule.
